Content With a Job

The Commercial SystemPart 9

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 9-minute read · Growth

In short: A piece of B2B content has a job when you can name its reader, the decision it helps that reader make, the stage of the purchase it serves and the action that should follow. Most libraries fail that test: Forrester found sales reps choosing from an average of 1,400 assets, and Gartner found 69% of buyers report inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers tell them. Two shifts make the job more specific than it used to be. Search sends fewer clicks, so content must be the source an answer cites; and buying groups average about 13 people, so content must help one buyer make the case to the rest.

Key points

  • A content job has four parts: a named reader, a decision, a buying stage and a next action.
  • Libraries grow faster than they are used; Forrester found reps had an average of 1,400 sales assets to choose from.
  • Pew found Google users clicked a result on 8% of visits with an AI summary, against 15% without one.
  • Buying groups of about 13 people mean much content is read by someone the seller never meets.
  • Every piece needs an owner, a measure that fits its job and a retirement date, or it becomes a liability.

Part 8 treated demand as an economic chain from spend to cash. Content sits inside that chain as one of the main forms of demand creation, and it has the same weakness as every creation channel: its effect is slow, diffuse and easy to dismiss. The answer is not to measure content harder. It is to commission it more precisely, so that each piece has a job someone can check.

Our earlier piece on owned channels argued that every piece should answer a buyer's search, explain a contrarian belief or provide a reusable tool. This part takes that idea down a level, to the brief, the measure and the decision to retire.

The library nobody can find a use for

Content libraries grow by accretion. A campaign needs a guide, a launch needs a deck, an event needs a summary, and each is kept because deleting feels like waste. Forrester's 2022 analysis of sales content found reps had an average of 1,400 sales assets to choose from, that the gap between what sales organisations thought was impactful and what sellers actually used had widened, and that sales playbooks showed low influence and low use throughout the buying journey.

Volume creates a second problem: inconsistency. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them. Old content does not just sit unused. It contradicts the current position, and buyers notice. Part 2 of this series covered positioning; content that has drifted from it undoes the work.

AI has made the volume problem worse. Our piece Judgment is the moat covers the evidence that teams are publishing more because drafting is cheaper. The Content Marketing Institute and MarketingProfs' 2026 survey of 861 B2B marketers found 88% said their organisation uses AI-powered content creation tools, and 65% said they had faced more pressure to produce content faster in the previous 12 months. Ensuring accuracy and maintaining quality control were the most cited AI content problems, each at 54%. Cheaper drafts lower the cost of a piece without lowering the cost of a reader's attention, or of a contradiction.

What a job is

A content job is a sentence with four slots: this reader, at this stage, needs to decide this, and should then do this. If any slot is blank, the piece does not have a job yet.

The stages matter because buyers need different things at different points. Forrester's analysis found features, functions and industry trends most influential early in the journey, while pricing and implementation options mattered more at the commit stage. The roles matter because the buying group is large and mixed. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments.

StageTypical readerDecision they faceContent that does the jobNext action
ProblemSponsor or userIs this problem worth solving now?Sizing piece with a cost the reader can check against their own numbersShare internally; book a conversation
ApproachSponsorWhich way of solving it fits us?Method comparison that names when each option is wrongShortlist an approach
SupplierEvaluation leadWhich supplier, and why?Proof: case evidence, references, a sample deliverableRequest a proposal
RiskFinance, IT, legalCan we afford it, secure it, sign it?Pricing logic, security answers, contract terms explainedClear their part of the approval
CommitSponsorWill it work here, on our timeline?Implementation plan with the first 90 days and named dependenciesSign
ValueUser and account ownerAre we getting what we paid for?Onboarding guide, outcome review templateRenew or expand

The table exposes the usual gap. Most libraries are heavy in the first two rows, because that is where marketing has traditionally worked, and thin in the risk row, where the finance director or security lead the seller never meets decides whether the deal moves. Content for those readers is often the most valuable a firm can produce and the least likely to be commissioned.

If you cannot say who reads it, what they decide and what they do next, the piece does not have a job. It has a topic.

Why the job has changed

Two shifts make the job more demanding than it was five years ago.

Fewer clicks reach the page. Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults' Google searches in March 2025 and found users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% when one did not. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025. Publishers are not B2B suppliers, and the report notes it is unclear how much of the fall is due to AI summaries, but the direction is consistent. Content whose job was "rank and get the click" now has to be the source the summary draws on. Our pieces on how LLMs choose sources and what SEO is now cover the mechanics.

More of the reading happens without the seller. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Gartner's analyst noted that sellers "can't rely on static collateral to carry influence in those moments." This is not new: Gartner reported in 2018 that B2B buyers spent just 17% of their buying time meeting suppliers, and about two-thirds researching and talking with peers independently. McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey found the supplier's website was among the most used touchpoints. The practical consequence is that a piece must survive being forwarded to someone with no context, read in isolation or summarised by a model. It needs to state its claim early, carry its own evidence and make the next step obvious.

The job brief

Every commissioned piece should start with a one-page brief. It takes ten minutes to write and saves the commissioning conversation that otherwise happens after the draft.

FieldWhat goes in itWhy it matters
ReaderOne role, not "decision makers"Sets vocabulary, depth and what can be assumed
StageOne row from the table aboveStops a piece trying to serve the whole journey
DecisionThe question the reader must answerDefines what the piece must contain to be useful
EvidenceThe facts, cases or numbers the piece will useSeparates a claim from an opinion
Next actionWhat the reader should do after readingGives the piece a measurable outcome
OwnerThe person who keeps it accurateSomeone is accountable when it drifts
MeasureThe signal that shows it did its jobChosen to fit the job, not the channel
Review dateWhen it will be checked against current positioningBuilds retirement into the plan

The brief also forces a choice about where the piece lives. Problem and approach content is usually public, because it must be found. Risk and commit content is often better as a controlled document a seller sends, because it is specific and changes with the offer. Our explainer on what makes a case study believable covers the supplier-stage row in more detail.

Measuring a piece against its job

The measure follows from the job, which is why pageviews are rarely the right one. A problem-sizing piece is doing its job if it is shared inside target accounts and precedes first meetings. A security answers document is doing its job if deals stop stalling at the security review. An implementation plan is doing its job if sellers attach it to late-stage opportunities and the time from proposal to signature falls.

Three measures cover most jobs:

  1. Sales use. How often the piece is sent or attached in open opportunities, taken from the CRM or the sales content tool. A piece no seller sends in two quarters has either the wrong job or the wrong form.
  2. Stage effect. For opportunities where the piece was used, did the stage it serves move faster than for those where it was not? Volumes are often small, so read this as direction over two or three quarters, not as proof.
  3. Questions removed. Whether a recurring question in sales calls or the inbox stops recurring after the piece exists. This is the most direct test of a risk-row piece and the easiest to record.

Public content also earns a fourth measure: whether answer engines cite it for the questions in its brief. That is checked by asking them, periodically, and recording the result. Our piece Stop reporting reach makes the wider case for measures that show something happened rather than that something was seen.

Retiring content

The review date in the brief is where most content programmes fail, because nobody owns deletion. A quarterly audit fixes it. For each piece past its review date, the owner makes one of four calls: keep, refresh, merge into a stronger piece, or retire. Pieces with no owner are retired by default.

The test for retirement is not age. It is whether the piece still matches the current position, offer and evidence. A three-year-old method comparison can be the best piece in the library; a three-month-old launch page for a discontinued package is a liability. Given Gartner's 69% inconsistency finding, a contradiction is worse than a gap.

Treat each retirement or major refresh as a small decision worth recording: what changed, why, who decided. Over a year, that record shows which jobs the firm keeps needing, which it keeps getting wrong, and where the library has holes. The owned channels argument about compounding applies only to content that is maintained. Unmaintained content does not compound. It decays.

Illustrative example: filling the risk row
Decision
Commission three risk-stage pieces (pricing logic, security answers and a contract terms explainer) and retire 40 problem-stage pieces with no seller use in two quarters.
Reason and owner
Win-loss notes showed deals stalling after the sponsor agreed, at finance and security review, while the library held almost nothing for those readers. Owned by the head of marketing, with each piece owned by the relevant specialist.
What changed
Sellers began attaching the security answers document to most late-stage deals, and the recurring security questionnaire call was dropped from the standard process.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software and services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

lowob takeaways

  • Write the job before the piece. Reader, stage, decision and next action, in one sentence.
  • Fill the risk row. Finance, security and legal readers decide deals and are rarely written for.
  • Write for the forward and the summary. Claim first, evidence included, next step obvious.
  • Measure against the job. Sales use, stage effect and questions removed beat pageviews.
  • Own deletion. A quarterly audit with retirement by default for pieces without an owner.
Gateway card

Before you commission the next piece

  • A named reader role and a single buying stage
  • The decision the reader faces, written as a question
  • The evidence the piece will use, listed before drafting starts
  • A next action and the measure that will show it happened
  • A named owner and a review date
  • A check that it does not contradict current positioning

Common questions

How do you create a B2B content strategy?

Start from the decisions buyers face at each stage of a purchase and the roles in the buying group, then commission content for the gaps, each piece with a named reader, decision, next action, owner and review date.

How do you measure B2B content effectiveness?

Measure each piece against its job: how often sellers use it in open deals, whether the stage it serves moves faster, and whether the question it answers stops recurring. Pageviews rarely fit the job.

How often should you audit B2B content?

Quarterly is enough for most firms. Each piece past its review date is kept, refreshed, merged or retired, and pieces with no owner are retired by default.

How is AI search changing B2B content?

Fewer searches end in a click: Pew found 8% of visits with an AI summary led to a result click, against 15% without. Content now needs to be the source those summaries cite.
